Marty |last3=Zubko |first3=Pavlo |date=2022 |title=James Floyd Scott. 4 May 1942—6 April 2020 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |volume=73|pages=395–420 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.2021.0048 |s2cid=251257694 |doi-access=free }}</ref> (4 May 1942&nbsp;– 6 April 2020)<ref name="SAZU">{{cite web| url=http://www.sazu.si/clani/james-floyd-scott| title=James Floyd Scott| website=Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts| language=sl| access-date=16 October 2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Catalan |first1=Gustau |last2=Dawber |first2=Matthew |last3=Gregg |first3=Marty |last4=Morrison |first4=Finlay |last5=Ramesh |first5=Ramamoorthy |last6=Zubko |first6=Pavlo |date=2020 |title=James F. Scott (1942–2020) |journal=Nature Materials |language=en |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=580 |doi=10.1038/s41563-020-0692-x |bibcode=2020NatMa..19..580C |s2cid=218531247 |issn=1476-1122|doi-access=free |hdl=10261/233885 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> was an [[Americans|American]] [[physicist]] and research director at the [[Cavendish Laboratory]], [[University of Cambridge]].<ref name="cam">{{cite web | title=Prof. James Scott | website=Department of Physics, Cavendish Laboratory | url=http://www.qm.phy.cam.ac.uk/scott/ | access-date=16 October 2018 | archive-date=16 October 2018 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181016125953/http://www.qm.phy.cam.ac.uk/scott/ | url-status=dead }}</ref> He is considered one of the pioneers of [[Ferroelectric RAM|ferroelectric memory devices]]. He was elected to the [[Royal Society]] in 2008.<ref name="RS">{{cite web | title=JamesScott | website=Royal Society | date=19 September 2015 | url=https://royalsociety.org/people/james-scott-12247/ | access-date=16 October 2018}}</ref>

== Biography ==
James Scott was born in [[Beverly, New Jersey]]. He attended high school in New Jersey and graduated from [[Harvard University]] in 1963. After receiving his doctorate in physics from [[Ohio State University]] (1966) in the field of high resolution molecular [[spectroscopy]], he worked for six years in the Quantum Electronics Research Laboratory at [[Bell Labs|Bell Laboratories]], New Jersey. In 1972 he was appointed professor of physics at the [[University of Colorado]], Boulder, where he established a research program investigating [[Ferroelectricity|ferroelectrics]] using laser spectroscopy. It was here that began his groundbreaking work on "integrated ferroelectrics" &mdash; semiconductor chips that incorporate thin ferroelectric memory devices. In 1984 he co-founded [[Symetrix]] Corporation to develop [[ferroelectric RAM]] (FRAM), which licensed its technology to [[Matsushita Electric|Matsushita]]. There followed appointments as Dean at the [[RMIT University|Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology]] (1992) and the [[University of New South Wales]] (1995). In 1997, he worked as a visiting professor in [[Yokohama]] thanks to an award from [[Sony]] and in [[Germany]] after receiving a [[Humboldt Prize|Humboldt Research Award]]. In 1999, when he left Symetrix, he became professor of [[ferroics]] at the [[University of Cambridge]] where his research focused on multiferoed magnetoelectrics and nanometric methods.<ref name="SAZU" /> From 2015 he was a joint professor in both chemistry and physics at the [[University of St Andrews]].

James Scott died on 6 April 2020, leaving a wife and three children.<ref>{{cite web |title=James (Jim) Scott 1942 - 2020 |url=https://www.phy.cam.ac.uk/news/james-jim-scott-1942-2020 |website=University of Cambridge Department of Physics |date=8 April 2020 |publisher=University of Cambridge |access-date=10 April 2020}}</ref>

== Awards ==
He was awarded the [[Materials Research Society]] gold medal in 2008 and Slovenia's [[Josef Stefan|Jožef Stefan]] gold medal in 2009.<ref name="cam" /> He was a member of the [[American Physical Society]] from 1974, a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] from 2008,<ref name="RS" /> and a member of the [[Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts]] since 2011.<ref name="cam" /> In 2014 he was listed by Thomson Reuters as [[Clarivate Citation Laureates|among the most highly cited physicists]].<ref name="TRCL">{{cite web | title=Physics | website=sciencewatch.com | date=24 April 2016 | url=http://sciencewatch.com/nobel/2014-predictions/physics-laureates | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160424230439/http://sciencewatch.com/nobel/2014-predictions/physics-laureates | archive-date=24 April 2016 | url-status=unfit | access-date=16 October 2018}}</ref> In 2016 he was awarded the UNESCO medal for contributions to nanoscience and nanotechnology.
